title: Incremental tokenizer prefetch and backpressure proposal
body:
Purpose
This doc proposes an incremental tokenizer prefetcher and backpressure model that sits at the tokenizer/runtime boundary. Goal: reduce observed tail tokenization latency for short and medium inputs, allow safe batching without increasing end-to-end P95, and coordinate with the KV cache so tokenization work avoids redundant work and minimizes duplicated KV lookups.

Context and motivation
- We currently observe two recurring pain points: (1) tokenization CPU spikes that create latency tail at low QPS when many concurrent small requests arrive; (2) redundant tokenizer work when requests hit the same prefixes or when retry/fallback logic re-tokenizes identical text.
- Prior notes exist on batching and tokenization cache; this draft focuses on a lightweight prefetching proxy and explicit backpressure signals for the serving runtime scheduler.

Non-goals
- This is not a full replacement for model-level KV cache strategies (e.g., server-side prefix caching inside kernel). It complements them by reducing tokenization overhead and aligning tokenization work with existing KV cache keys.

Design principles
- Low friction: opt-in switch at route/config level; default safe behavior is unchanged.
- Bounded speculation: prefetch windows and CPU budget limits prevent tokenization from stealing cycles from model inference.
- Idempotency: avoid changing request semantics — tokenization results must be deterministic and cached safely.
- Observability: per-request tokenization time, prefetch budget used, cache hits, and backpressure events must be emitted.

High-level design
1) Tokenization Proxy (lightweight process/library)
- Sits co-located with the serving runtime process (same host/container) and exposes a small sync/async interface: tokenize(text, options) -> tokens + metadata.
- Responsibilities:
  - Maintain an in-memory LRU keyed by text-sha256 -> tokenization result (tokens, token_count, token_lengths, normalized_text). TTL: configurable (default 5m) with sloppy expiry.
  - Support prefix-keyed cache: store canonicalized prefixes so tokenization of incremental appends can reuse prefix tokens.
  - Implement a prefetcher that speculatively tokenizes continuations for streaming requests: given a request size and history, it can pre-tokenize likely next chunks (configurable window in bytes/tokens).
  - Emit backpressure hints to the scheduler when CPU or tokenization queue depth passes thresholds.

2) Prefetch policy and budget
- Budget style: per-instance soft budget expressed in ms/sec (e.g., allow up to 50ms of speculative tokenization work per second per core). This prevents runaway speculation.
- Prefetch window: max N tokens or M characters ahead. Configurable by route/model. Smaller windows for low-latency routes.
- Priority: real-request tokenization always beats speculative prefetch in the queue. Prefetch tasks are low priority and can be canceled if model-inference queue grows.

3) Backpressure signals to scheduler
- Three-level signals emitted by Tokenization Proxy: OK, SOFT_LIMIT, HARD_LIMIT.
  - OK: normal operation.
  - SOFT_LIMIT: prefetching paused; scheduler should avoid creating large tokenization batches for new low-latency routes; consider increasing priority for model workers.
  - HARD_LIMIT: refuse speculative tokenization; shed speculative tasks; optionally reject low-priority requests with specific error code that the caller can retry with backoff.
- Scheduler integration: scheduler maintains per-host tokenization_utilization metric and uses signals to shape admission control for new requests and to influence batching decisions (e.g., avoid growing tokenization batch sizes when under SOFT/HARD).

4) KV cache interplay
- Cache keys alignment: Tokenization Proxy normalizes text exactly as keys used by model-side KV cache (same normalization pipeline: whitespace, special tokens, case where applicable) so prefix caches map 1:1 to KV cache prefixes.
- On cache-missing paths, the proxy can optionally emit a hint for the KV cache to pre-warm on next token range (configurable via route tags). This is advisory; the KV layer decides whether to act.
- Duplicate tokenization avoidance: if the runtime obtains KV cache hits for some prefix, the proxy will skip tokenization for that prefix and only produce tokens for the uncached suffix to avoid duplicate CPU + KV lookups. This requires a small API handshake: model runtime can answer 'prefix cached up to token index K' (handshake messages documented below).

API handshake (lightweight)
- tokenize_request -> {text, request_id, history_hash, want_prefetch: bool}
- tokenize_response -> {tokens, normalized_text, prefix_cached_up_to: int}
- runtime_prefix_status (optional) -> {request_id, cached_upto_token_index}
- Prefetch tasks tagged with originating_request_id to cancel when runtime signals that cached prefix exists.

Batching strategies and partial merges
- Partial-merge batches: group tokenization of multiple requests that share initial bytes into a single canonicalization step. For example, for three requests that start with common 100 chars, the proxy canonicalizes the common prefix once and branches for the suffixes. This reduces duplicated work but increases code complexity—opt-in per deployment.
- Hybrid batching: small requests (< X tokens) are grouped into micro-batches up to a small wall-clock timeout (Y ms). Larger requests bypass micro-batching. Backpressure signals reduce micro-batch timeouts when tokenization_utilization high.

Metrics and signals to track
- per_request_tokenize_ms (p50/p95/p99)
- speculative_tokenize_ms_total
- prefetch_tasks_started / cancelled
- token_cache_hit_ratio (exact text key and prefix key)
- tokenization_utilization (ms/sec per core)
- backpressure_events (soft/hard) and downstream effects on end-to-end latency

Safety and failure modes
- Determinism: tokenization cache keys must be computed using a canonicalization function identical to downstream consumers. Any change is a rollout risk.
- Memory pressure: LRU size must be tuned; use soft eviction and metrics to alert when eviction rate high.
- SLO interactions: prefetch should never increase tail latency for critical low-latency routes. Use route-level flags to disable prefetch on high-SLA routes.

Experiments to run (initial roadmap)
- A/B: enable prefetch on a small percentage of hosts for a single low-latency public route. Measure P50/P95/P99 tokenization and end-to-end latency, as well as CPU utilization.
- Prefix cache effectiveness: sample corpus from production logs and simulate prefix hit rates with different TTLs and LRU sizes.
- Backpressure tuning: stress test with bursty arrivals to validate SOFT/HARD thresholds.

Migration and rollout plan
1) Implement Tokenization Proxy library and a basic in-memory LRU. Unit tests for canonicalization.
2) Integrate backpressure signal to scheduler as a non-blocking hint. Expose route flag "enable_prefetch_v1".
3) Run canary for 5% traffic on non-critical routes, observe metrics for 2 weeks.
4) If stable, expand to more services and enable partial-merge batching as opt-in.

Open questions / tradeoffs
- How to ensure the canonicalization function stays in sync across repo boundaries? Suggest a shared library or a generated canonicalizer from a single source of truth.
- Is it acceptable to have model runtime return prefix cache hits in the hot path? This adds RPCs/handshake complexity.
- Cost tradeoff of extra speculative CPU vs saved inference KV lookups: run cost simulation.

Next steps / TODOs
- [ ] Spike implementation of proxy with LRU and simple prefetcher (owner: Maya)
- [ ] Prototype scheduler hook + backpressure metric (owner: Rafael)
- [ ] Create Linear tickets for canary and A/B experiments (Priya)
- [ ] Draft runbook for prefetch-induced memory/CPU alerts (Liam)

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally conservative: speculation is bounded and opt-in. Looking for feedback on handshake API and suggested default budgets. Also open to alternate naming ("tokenization prefetcher" vs "tokenization proxy").

References and inspirations
- Prior tokenization notes: TKN-103, TKN-221 (see linked linear issues)
- Internal PR: serving-runtime/pull/879 contains an early tokenizer cache prototype.

End of doc"
